Great horned owls (Bubo virginianus) exhibit a well-defined developmental trajectory during the early post-hatching period. Eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] produce hatchlings after a documented incubation period of approximately 27 days [ab = approximately 27 days], a duration that aligns closely with values reported for other large North American strigiforms. At the moment of hatching, the altricial nestlings are remarkably small, with a recorded wet weight at birth of 34.7 grams [Wwb = 34.7 grams]. This minimal starting mass reflects the substantial energetic investment that the species must direct to rapid body growth during the subsequent nestling phase. The initial 27-day development within the egg, thermoregulated by the incubating adult at a consistent 36 °C [T = 36 °C], represents a critical period of organogenesis. Immediately following emergence, the downy chicks are entirely dependent on parental provisioning for both food and warmth. The relatively modest neonatal mass is a characteristic trait of this species, setting the stage for a pronounced growth trajectory that will continue until the individuals approach their adult dimensions.

Sexual size dimorphism is pronounced in Bubo virginianus, a pattern common among raptorial birds where females attain substantially larger ultimate body dimensions than males. Field surveys and morphometric analyses of adult specimens have established that females reach an ultimate wet weight of 1608 grams [Wwi = 1608 grams], whereas adult males achieve a considerably lower ultimate wet weight of 1224 grams [Wwi = 1224 grams]. This disparity of nearly 400 grams is thought to be an adaptive response to the energetic demands of egg production and incubation in females, while the smaller male mass may facilitate greater agility during hunting. The asymptotic mass for both sexes is typically attained by the end of the first full year of life, after the completion of the juvenile growth phase. Such a marked difference in adult body mass influences multiple aspects of the species' ecology, including prey selection, territory size, and parental roles during the breeding season. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this degree of dimorphism is typical within the genus Bubo.

Under the thermal conditions characteristic of the species' active metabolic state, specifically a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], several key life-history milestones are reached according to a predictable schedule. The nestling period culminates in fledging, a critical behavioral transition marked by the first sustained flight, which occurs approximately 46 days after hatching [tx = approximately 46 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This fledging age is consistent with the prolonged developmental period typical of large strigiforms, which balances the need for flight feather maturation against the substantial predation risk inherent in extended nest occupancy. Following successful fledging, the young owls remain in a dependent juvenile stage, gradually refining their hunting skills under the tutelage of the adults. This 46-day interval before fledging (46 days after hatching) [tx = 46 days after hatching] enables the young to attain sufficient flight feather development and body mass before leaving the nest at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The developmental pace is facilitated by a high metabolic rate and efficient food conversion, allowing young owls to depart the nest with sufficient body mass and feather development to survive the immediate post-fledging challenges.

The onset of reproductive capability in Great horned owls is delayed relative to the attainment of adult body size, reflecting the significant behavioral and physiological maturation required for successful breeding. Under the standard active thermoregulatory regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the time since birth at puberty has been estimated at 138 days [tp = 138 days]. This timing indicates that gonadal maturation and the associated hormonal cascades commence relatively soon after fledging, though actual breeding is typically deferred much longer. The 138-day milestone (138 days since birth) [tp = 138 days since birth] marks the physiological readiness for reproduction, but the acquisition of a suitable territory, the formation of a pair bond, and the attainment of full hunting proficiency often delay the first actual breeding attempt by many additional months at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Data on this pubertal timing derive from histological examinations of gonadal tissue and monitoring of plasma hormone levels. The species' relatively late sexual maturation is a common life-history strategy among long-lived, top-predator birds of prey.

The reproductive schedule of Bubo virginianus is characterized by a single annual breeding event, with the first successful brood typically occurring at a relatively advanced age. Under the species' normal body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the time since birth at first brood is approximately 730 days [tR = approximately 730 days], or roughly two years after hatching. This substantial delay between reaching sexual maturity and producing the first clutch reflects the demanding requirements of territory establishment, nest site selection, and pair bonding. Females typically lay one to three eggs per clutch, producing exactly one clutch each year, corresponding to a maximum reproduction rate of approximately 3 fledglings per year [Ri = approximately 3 fledglings per year]. This conservative reproductive rate, combined with the late onset of breeding, is typical of long-lived raptors. The species' longevity supports this slow reproductive tempo: maximum recorded lifespan in the wild reaches 29 years [am = 29 years], with these observations consistently made at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].
